topic: weaving willow baskets: soaking brown rods, stake spacing and rolling a level border

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-5)
provenance.notes: pisane niezaleznie, nie jest tlumaczeniem; urzadzenie obliczeniowe: termometr z zapisem w kadzi do moczenia

base: I have started weaving willow baskets and my rods keep cracking at the tight bends.
An old log basket by the hearth was woven by my grandmother and has never split.
A recording thermometer stands in the soaking tank and marks the water every hour.
I soaked this year's brown rods for four days before I began to weave them.
Is four days too short, or am I bending the rods the wrong way entirely?
Four days is short for brown rods, which want a week and then a night mellowing.
Soaking softens the bark and the pith together, and the pith takes the longest.
Wrap the drained rods in wet sacking overnight so the moisture spreads right through.
Cold water needs far longer than warm, which is why the season matters so much.
I soaked the next bundle for a week and mellowed it overnight in damp sacking.
The thermometer shows the tank sitting at six degrees, which is colder than I assumed.
The rods now bend without cracking, though the weave looks looser than the log basket.
Should I beat the weave down harder, or is the looseness coming from the stakes?
It is the stakes, almost certainly, because a loose weave follows from stakes set too far apart.
Beating harder on wide stakes only bruises the rods and leaves the sides slack anyway.
Count your stakes against the width of the base and add two if they look sparse.
A tight base carries the whole basket, and no amount of later work will save a slack one.
I added four stakes and the sides came up much firmer than on the first basket.
The border, though, keeps rising unevenly and one side stands a finger higher.
The old log basket has a flat border that looks as though it was rolled in one pass.
Is that a trick of the border weave, or did she trim it flat afterwards?
No trimming; a rolled border comes out flat only if every stake is soaked equally.
Stakes that dried while you worked will spring back and lift that side of the rim.
Keep a wet cloth over the standing work and damp the stakes before you start the border.
Work the border in one sitting, since a break of an hour is enough to spoil it.
Damping the stakes worked and the border came out level all the way round.
The basket has dried for a fortnight and the whole weave has shrunk a little.
Two rods have loosened near the handle and rattle slightly when I lift the thing.
Can I tighten those rods now, or is the basket best left as it stands?
Leave them, because dry willow will crack the moment you try to drive it tighter.
Shrinkage of that order is normal and stops once the basket reaches the air of the room.
Next time weave a shade tighter than feels right, allowing for what the drying takes back.
The handle bow is the one place worth binding again, since it carries all the weight.
I bound the handle bow again with fresh skeins and it feels solid under a full load.
The basket carried a bushel of apples last week without any sign of spreading.
I would like to cut my own rods next winter rather than buy them by the bundle.
When should the cutting be done, and how long must the rods stand before use?
Cut after the leaf falls and before the sap rises, so any time from December onward.
Stand the bundles upright outdoors until the rods have dried right through to the pith.
That usually takes a good three months, and only then are they worth soaking.
Rods used green shrink in the finished work and leave you exactly where you started.
